title: SMYD3-catalyzed dimethylation of gasdermin D at lysine 43 promotes pyroptosis and inflammatory responses.
Sensitivity of stochastic growth rate and lifetime reproductive output to kin effects: A nonlinear feedback model
summary: Humans exhibit a coevolutionary relationship between the trajectory of social evolution and senescence. A focal individual's kinship network is a function of his/her life history, while that network in turn shapes the focal individual's life history through kin effects on reproduction, generating a dynamic, nonlinear feedback loop across the population. Assessing directional selection on kin effects, therefore, requires explicitly modelling the feedback between the kinship network and life history. Here, we develop such a framework and apply it to examine selection pressures on the cooperative behaviour of closely related kin, including mothers, grandmothers, and older sisters. We hypothesise that the negative association of grandmothers, mothers, and older sisters (>10 years) with child mortality are under positive selection because increasing the absolute values of these kin effects would increase the stochastic growth rate. Furthermore, we hypothesise that the positive association of older sisters with child mortality is subject to negative selection, as increasing this effect would reduce the stochastic growth rate. We estimate kin-specific slope coefficients for child mortality using a Bayesian hierarchical model and solve a system of nonlinear equations linking kinship structure and survival to account for the nonlinear feedback between kinship and child survival. Thereafter, we compute stochastic sensitivities of both the stochastic growth rate and the mean lifetime reproductive output to these slope coefficients. Consistent with our hypotheses, all slope coefficients for kin presence on child mortality are negatively sensitive to both fitness metrics. We discuss the applications of our framework to examine the coevolution of social behaviours and senescence in age-structured populations.

title: Building Bridges Belowground: Pythium oligandrum En-hances Rhizosphere Network Connectivity
summary: Biological control agents (BCAs) offer a potential sustainable alternative to fungicides for crop dis-ease management, but their effects on resident plant microbiomes and microbial interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of the BCA Pythium oligandrum on disease con-trol and the rhizosphere microbiome of starch potato cv. Kuras in a field trial. We compared a labora-tory strain and a commercial formulation (Polygandron) with commonly used fungicides during early blight development. The laboratory strain suppressed early blight at plant senescence, but this effect did not persist until harvest, whereas fungicide treatment provided near-complete disease suppression throughout the growing season. P. oligandrum caused transient changes in rhizosphere fungal com-munity composition at flowering, while bacterial community richness varied among sampling times in untreated controls. However, bacterial co-occurrence network analysis revealed pronounced treat-ment-specific changes in microbial connectivity. Application of the laboratory strain increased net-work connectivity, resulting in almost a threefold increase in mean degree and greater interconnected-ness among bacterial taxa. In contrast, Polygandron and fungicide treatments reduced mean degree, indicating reduced connectivity within the bacterial network. Fungicide treatment additionally altered network organisation, including increased betweenness centrality and changes in modularity. Togeth-er, our results show that P. oligandrum can modify microbial interactions in the potato rhizosphere without substantially altering overall bacterial community composition, highlighting the value of in-tegrating microbial network structure with community-level analyses when evaluating the ecological effects of BCAs.

title: A finished, telomere-to-telomere assembly for Botrytis cinerea strain B05.10
summary: We present an improved genome assembly of Botrytis cinerea strain B05.10 which serves as a reference isolate for most labs active in the Botrytis research. The existing assembly dating from 2017 was extended by adding 8 telomeric regions and a small number of minor errors was corrected. The new assembly contains telomeres on each chromosome end, except for Chr4 carrying the rDNA repeat. The unannotated assembly is deposited in NCBI and manual curation of gene models is ongoing. The new assembly will be hosted on Ensembl-Fungi after completion of the structural curation.

title: Erythrocyte extravasation drives ferroptosis and inflammatory amplification in eccentric contraction-induced skeletal muscle injury via the heme-HO-1-iron axis
summary: Eccentric contraction-induced skeletal muscle injury is a common sports-related condition characterized by pain, impaired muscle function, slow recovery, and frequent recurrence, yet treatment remains symptomatic and mechanism-based targets are lacking. Although microvascular disruption and erythrocyte extravasation characterize severe muscle strain, the metabolic fate of extravasated erythrocytes has received little attention. In hemorrhagic and hemolytic conditions, erythrocyte-derived heme can activate heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1)-mediated iron release and ferroptosis, potentially amplifying inflammation; however, whether this pathway contributes to eccentric muscle injury remains unknown. To address this gap, we established a parameter-controlled rat model in which the gastrocnemius underwent 0, 50, 100, or 150 eccentric stretch repetitions. Muscle torque, gait, weight-bearing, endurance, pain threshold, histopathology, microcirculatory perfusion, macrophage polarization, and heme, ferrous iron, glutathione (GSH), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels were assessed. Increasing repetitions produced graded functional impairment, myofiber damage, erythrocyte extravasation, inflammatory infiltration, and microcirculatory disturbance. Heme accumulation was accompanied by HO-1 upregulation in perivascular CD68-positive (CD68) macrophages, muscle iron accumulation, GSH and GPX4 depletion, elevated MDA, and increased M1 macrophage and cytokine levels. These findings suggest a potential heme-HO-1-iron-ferroptosis-associated inflammatory mechanism in eccentric muscle injury, providing a rationale for mechanistic validation and targeted therapeutic development. Keywords: Eccentric contraction-induced muscle injury; Erythrocyte extravasation; Heme oxygenase-1; Ferroptosis; Macrophage polarization
